Incremental loss accumulation and pruning using a feasible upper bound are sensible search mechanisms. Detailed Haskell listings make the proposed implementation inspectable.

weaknesses: The implementation does not optimize the stated objective as written. Equation (1) counts zero predictions as errors, whereas loss01 gives them zero cost, and returned hyperplanes pass through training samples. No perturbation producing an actual classifier with the reported loss is constructed. The 1e-8 tolerance can also produce impossible optima: for one-dimensional points (1, 1+1e-9, 1+2e-9) labeled (+1, -1, +1), the code reports zero loss although every linear threshold makes at least one error.

The central correctness proof is invalid. Appendix A infers that greater Hamming distance from an optimal cell's sign vector implies greater loss against the true labels. This does not follow when the optimal classifier itself makes errors. Consequently, the claimed rigorous exactness guarantee is not established.

The claimed O(N^D) worst-case runtime contradicts the presented recursion. Without pruning, a prefix of size i contains binomial(i,D) completed models, each updated on the next observation. Summing these updates gives binomial(N,D+1), or Theta(N^(D+1)) for fixed D, before additional implementation costs. Upper-bound pruning does not establish a better worst-case bound.

The parameterization and linear solver introduce further correctness gaps. fitw fixes the intercept to +/-1 and assumes each selected raw-coordinate matrix is invertible. Affine general position does not guarantee this: the points (1,0), (2,0), and (0,1) are in general position, but the first pair produces a singular system. Singularities and non-general-position inputs are not handled.

The claim of the first polynomial-time exact algorithm for fixed dimension is not credible as positioned. Classical hyperplane-arrangement enumeration, followed by evaluation of each realizable dichotomy, already provides a polynomial-time approach for fixed dimension. strengths: Addresses a meaningful problem: globally minimizing empirical 0-1 loss for low-dimensional linear classifiers.
Provides detailed Haskell listings and a systematic derivation of combination enumeration and loss-based pruning, making the intended algorithm inspectable.
Reports comparisons on five UCI datasets, with lower stated error counts than standard classifiers on four datasets.
weaknesses: The central exactness claim is inconsistent with the stated objective. Equation (1) counts sign(0) as incorrect, whereas loss01 assigns zero loss to boundary predictions. For two one-dimensional points x=1,2 with labels -1,+1, either enumerated boundary incurs an error under Equation (1), while a threshold at 1.5 achieves zero errors. Constructing a suitable perturbation could repair this aspect, but the algorithm returns the unperturbed hyperplane. Appendix A also incorrectly assumes that greater Hamming distance from an optimal prediction vector implies greater loss against the true labels; optimality does not establish that ordering.

The advertised O(N^D) worst-case runtime is contradicted by the implementation. Without pruning, every candidate support requires evaluating all N observations, giving N·binom(N,D), or Ω(N^(D+1)), point evaluations for fixed D. Incremental updates distribute this work across iterations without eliminating it. No valid complexity analysis establishes the claimed improvement.

The numerical implementation can report an unattainable optimum even for data in general position. For distinct one-dimensional points 1, 1+10^-9, and 1+2·10^-9 with labels +1,-1,+1, the hard-coded 10^-8 tolerance makes every prediction zero for a candidate boundary, producing reported loss zero. Every actual linear threshold makes at least one error. Thus the exactness problem extends beyond merely omitting a final boundary perturbation.

The implementation requires assumptions stronger than the theorem states. fitw fixes the intercept and solves a square coordinate matrix, but affine general position does not guarantee that matrix is invertible. For example, the noncollinear points (1,0), (2,0), and (0,1) include a singular two-point support. The supplied rotatePivot routine can loop indefinitely on such a system. Degeneracies and their treatment in the UCI datasets are not addressed.

The claim to be the first polynomial-time exact algorithm for fixed dimension is inadequately positioned against classical hyperplane-arrangement algorithms, including the cited Edelsbrunner et al. work. Enumerating arrangement cells and evaluating their losses already provides a polynomial-time route in fixed dimension. The manuscript does not establish a distinct advance over that foundation.

The evaluation does not substantiate efficiency, exactness, or predictive superiority. Table 1 contains only five small, low-dimensional datasets, with no runtimes, memory measurements, scaling studies, pruning ablations, or comparisons against certified exact solvers. Preprocessing, baseline hyperparameters, and train/test protocols are unspecified. Lower empirical error against surrogate-loss methods neither certifies global optimality nor establishes better generalization, so the claims of practical replacement for SVMs and suitability for high-stakes prediction exceed the evidence.

The geometric enumeration perspective and monotone partial-loss pruning are useful algorithmic ingredients. Detailed Haskell listings make the proposed procedure inspectable.

The correctness proof contains an invalid inference. Appendix A assumes that greater Hamming distance from an optimal cell’s sign vector implies greater classification error against the true labels. Reports improved training accuracy over standard surrogate-loss methods on six small datasets, alongside several improvements in five-fold cross-validation test accuracy.
Includes runtime scaling experiments and quadratic-classification examples, while acknowledging the exponential dependence on dimension.
weaknesses: The central exactness theorem contradicts the stated objective. Equation (3), with sign(0)=0, counts boundary points as errors. For D=1, consider points x=(-1,1) with labels (-1,1): the classifier sign(x) has zero loss, but every enumerated threshold passing through a sample incurs at least one error. This directly contradicts Theorem 3. Likewise, a hyperplane containing exactly D samples satisfies E(w)+E(-w)=N+D, whereas Theorem 5 uses N-D. These errors invalidate the claimed guarantee and the algorithm's loss updates. Excluding boundary points would require a different scoring definition and a construction that produces an actual classifier attaining that score.

Theorem 3's proof incorrectly assumes that greater Hamming distance from an optimal cell's predictions implies greater error against the true labels. Optimality does not establish this monotonic relationship. A valid argument connecting vertex scores to realizable neighboring classifiers is missing.

The polynomial extension lacks a necessary assumption: general position in the original space does not imply general position after Veronese embedding. For example, six distinct points on a circle have no three collinear, but their quadratic lifts lie on one hyperplane in R^5. Consequently, Corollary 1 cannot directly invoke the preceding general-position argument, and the boundary-count assumption can also fail.

The pseudocode is not executable as specified. Algorithm 1 uses polynomial degree K to size and generate combinations but accesses D-combinations; polynomial classification requires G-combinations. It also initializes every combination list as empty, without the empty-subset base case. Algorithm 2 uses a stopping condition opposite to its stated purpose and calls ICE on the original dataset instead of the current block or coreset. No implementation link is provided to resolve these discrepancies; preprocessing, hardware, numerical tolerances, and coreset settings are also insufficiently documented.

Novelty over existing methods is not convincingly established. The manuscript acknowledges that PCS already enumerates D-point subsets. Changing the combination generator and exploiting orientation symmetry does not establish the claimed first provably correct standalone algorithm, especially given the proof defects. Direct comparisons with PCS and ablations isolating these changes are absent.

The runtime superiority claim exceeds the evidence. The approximately 317-year branch-and-bound runtime is extrapolated from a fitted curve, not measured, and does not establish worst-case behavior. Comparisons concentrate on three-dimensional synthetic data and MATLAB implementations of an older branch-and-bound method and GLPK, without sufficient implementation and hardware controls or evaluation against a stronger contemporary MIP solver.

The generalization conclusions are overstated. A smaller VC upper bound does not guarantee better actual test error. Only six rows in Table 2 concern exact optimization; the remaining eight use an approximate coreset wrapper and therefore cannot establish benefits attributable to global optimality. Among the exact results, ICE loses to a baseline on two datasets, and several gains are small relative to reported variability. These findings do not support the broad claim that the work refutes concerns about overfitting.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: exact empirical 0–1 loss minimization for low-dimensional linear classifiers, while acknowledging the exponential dependence on dimension.
The geometric perspective connecting classification, point–hyperplane duality, and arrangement faces is useful, and the illustrations help explain the proposed search.

Experiments include linear and quadratic classification, runtime measurements, and cross-validation. Table 2 explicitly distinguishes claimed exact solutions from approximate coreset results, and several reported improvements merit further investigation.
weaknesses: The central optimality theorem is false under the stated objective. Equation (3) and the definition sign(0)=0 count every boundary point as misclassified. Consider D=1, points x=(0,1,2), and labels (+1,−1,+1), which satisfy general position. Every enumerated threshold through a data point makes two errors in either orientation, whereas a threshold below all three points makes only one. This contradicts Theorem 3. Likewise, with D boundary points, the correct identity is E(−w)=N+D−E(w), not N−D−E(w) as stated in Theorem 5 and implemented in Algorithm 1. The latter incorrectly reports zero errors in this example. Excluding boundary points would change the objective and require a proved construction of an actual classifier attaining the reported loss.

The Appendix A proof of Theorem 3 additionally assumes that greater disagreement with an optimal cell's sign vector implies greater disagreement with the true labels. Optimality does not establish this monotonic relationship between Hamming distances. Consequently, the proof needs substantive repair beyond changing the boundary convention.

The polynomial extension does not justify its general-position assumption. General position in the original space does not imply general position after Veronese embedding: six distinct points on a circle have no three collinear, but their quadratic lifts into R^5 all satisfy the affine relation x₁²+x₂²=1. Corollary 1 therefore cannot directly invoke the linear theorem under its stated assumptions. Degeneracies in real datasets also lack an explicit treatment.

The novelty claim is insufficiently established. The manuscript acknowledges that PCS already enumerates hyperplanes through D-point subsets, but does not adequately distinguish its contribution from that method or classical constructive hyperplane-arrangement algorithms, including the cited Edelsbrunner et al. work. Polynomial feature lifting is standard, and adopting a different combination generator does not by itself substantiate the claim of the first standalone exact algorithm.

The runtime evidence does not support the strongest superiority claims. The comparison of 1.2 seconds against 317 years extrapolates fitted runtime curves far beyond the measured BnB instances; it is not a demonstrated worst-case comparison. Empirical curve fitting cannot establish exponential worst-case complexity. The GLPK comparison also lacks sufficient formulation, solver-setting, and hardware details, and stronger contemporary exact-solver baselines are absent.

The generalization conclusions exceed the evidence. A VC upper bound does not imply that lower empirical error orders classifiers by test error. Among the six rows marked exact in Table 2, ICE loses to LDA on HA and SVM on CR, while several gains are small relative to the reported variation. The larger-dataset results use approximate stochastic coresets and therefore do not establish benefits caused by global optimality. The evaluation also lacks a sufficiently specified validation protocol and statistical comparison to support the broad claims.

Reproducibility is inadequate for checking the claimed guarantees. Algorithm 1 allocates and generates combinations using polynomial degree K but accesses Css[D], although polynomial classification requires combinations of size G; its initialization also fails to seed the empty combination. Algorithm 2 uses while |C|≤B_max, which skips filtering oversized inputs. No implementation link is provided, and dataset preprocessing, feature selection, numerical boundary handling, and coreset settings are insufficiently documented. These issues prevent a reliable reconstruction and independent verification of the reported results.
